answer.html: A communications satellite is a projectile that falls around Earth. 𝑣= √G𝑚<sup>E</sup> / 𝑟 is the speed at which its fall matches Earth's curvature, and 𝑇= 2𝜋√𝑟<sup>3</sup> / G𝑚<sup>E</sup> tells how long one lap takes. Gravity is still strong there (about 14% weaker than at the surface at the station's height), so the satellite is not "escaping gravity": it is in free fall. answer.html: The mass does not change; it is the amount of matter (and the rover's inertia). Its weight 𝑚𝑔 changes: it is largest on Earth (𝑔= 9.80 N/kg), decreases in space as the distance from Earth grows, and settles to a smaller value on Mars (3.71 N/kg).

items.title: Figure 13 prompt, Explain why the gravitational pull of the Sun on a spacecraft never becomes exactly zero, even beyond Pluto.

answer.html: 𝑔= G𝑚/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup> gets smaller as 𝑟 grows but is zero only if 𝑟 is infinite (or 𝑚= 0). At any finite distance, even far beyond Pluto, the Sun's field has a nonzero value, so the pull becomes very small but never reaches zero.

items.title: Get It? (fields), Explain how the field concept describes the way the Moon causes ocean tides without touching the water.

answer.html: The Moon sets up a gravitational field in the space around it, 𝑔= G𝑚<sub>M</sub> / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>, pointing toward the Moon. The ocean water at Earth feels a force from the field at its own location (𝐹<sub>g</sub> = 𝑚𝑔 ), stronger on the side facing the Moon, so the Moon influences the water without any contact.

items.title: Figure 16 prompt, Describe how the bending of starlight passing near the Sun contradicts your experience of light's behavior.

answer.html: In everyday life, light travels in straight lines. General relativity says light follows curved space near a massive object, so starlight passing close to the Sun bends and the star appears shifted from its true position (seen during a solar eclipse). We never notice this on Earth because ordinary gravity is far too weak to bend light noticeably.

items.title: Check Your Progress 22, Newton's second law is called a law, while general relativity's explanation of gravitational waves is a theory. Explain the difference.

answer.html: Newton's second law (𝐹= 𝑚𝑎) describes what happens: how acceleration depends on force and mass. It does not explain why nature behaves that way. General relativity is a theory because it explains why gravity acts as it does: mass curves space, and changes in that curvature travel as gravitational waves. A theory also makes broad, testable predictions (the wave detections by LIGO confirmed one), while a law is a compact summary of a pattern.

items.title: Scientific Breakthroughs, 3D Thinking: "Use a Model to Illustrate" how astronomers detect an unseen planet from its pull on its star

body.html: A planet and its star both orbit their common center of mass, so the planet's gravity makes the star wobble. The wobble shows up as a small, repeating Doppler shift of the star's light.

For a Jupiter-mass planet at 5.2 AU from a Sun-like star, the planet moves at 𝑣<sup>p</sup> = √G𝑚<sup>S</sup> / 𝑟= 1.31 × 10<sup>4</sup> m/s. The star's speed is smaller by the mass ratio 𝑚<sub>J</sub> / 𝑚<sub>S</sub> = 9.55 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup>:

answer.html: Draw the star and planet orbiting a point near the star, with arrows showing the star's small velocity. Label "star moving toward us: light shifts blue" and "star moving away: light shifts red," and plot the repeating shift against time. A detected 12.5 m/s wobble with a period matching Kepler's third law reveals the planet and its mass. (Class presentation; the number is a sample.)

items.title: Scientific Breakthroughs, 3D Thinking: "Use a Model to Illustrate" how a LIGO detects gravitational waves

body.html: A LIGO is a giant laser interferometer: a laser beam is split into two perpendicular arms several km long. Mirrors at the ends reflect the beams back, where they recombine. Without a wave, the arms are equal and the light cancels at the detector.

A passing gravitational wave stretches one arm and squeezes the other by an extremely small amount (less than a proton's width). The path lengths differ slightly, the recombined light no longer cancels, and the detector sees a signal. Two (or three) separated observatories confirm it and triangulate the source.

answer.html: Draw a laser, beam splitter, two perpendicular arms with mirrors, and a photodetector. Label "no wave: beams cancel" and "wave: arm lengths change, light reaches detector." (Class presentation; no numerical answer.)
